title: Rohatsu
hook: the week of sitting before December 8

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kathina a third time: a robe sewn like rice fields and used until the last shreds went into the plaster. Your line: the robe given.

What shows up when you sit still for a long time? Not two minutes. Days. In Japanese Zen, the week that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening is called Rohatsu: a week of sitting, from before dawn into the night. Last year you met its end, the last night and the morning star. This year, stay in the middle, the long hours when the mind brings out everything it has. An old poem has a name for all of it.
screen: `WHAT SHOWS UP IN A LONG SIT?` → `A WEEK OF SITTING.` → `AN OLD POEM NAMES IT.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Padhana Sutta, the discourse on striving, in the Sutta Nipata. The young seeker is by a river, worn thin from effort, and Mara comes to him. Not with weapons. Kindly. You're thin, he says. You're close to death. Live, and do good deeds. Why wear yourself out? It's a reasonable voice. That's the trouble with it. The seeker answers by naming Mara's army, one troop at a time. Desires. Discontent. Hunger and thirst. Craving. Sloth and drowsiness. Fear. Doubt. Hypocrisy and stubbornness. Gain, fame and honor, and praising yourself while looking down on others. There isn't a monster in that list. It's the inside of a long sit: aching legs, and the voice that says this is pointless. Hunger an hour before lunch. Sleep pulling at the eyelids after midday. Doubt asking who you think you are. A little pride, too, about how well you're sitting. The poem's weapon isn't force. The seeker will break this army with wisdom, the way a stone breaks an unbaked clay pot: see each troop clearly, name it, and not get up. In the poem's own picture, he would rather fall in battle than live on defeated. At the end, Mara gives up. His lute slips from under his arm, and he disappears. So Rohatsu isn't only endurance. It's the same scene played again, in a cold hall, by ordinary people, the troops arriving on schedule and named as they come.
screen: `MARA ARRIVES KINDLY.` · `THE SEEKER NAMES THE ARMY.` · `IT'S THE INSIDE OF A LONG SIT.` · then, large: `SEE IT, NAME IT, DON'T GET UP.`

segments.voice: As each thing turns up, name it quietly with the poem's words: desire, discontent, hunger, sleepiness, fear, doubt. Name it, and stay where you are. You don't have to win; you only have to notice and not get up.
Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, when the old army comes and gets named. Today's word.
Your line: the week of sitting. The army comes, and the seeker stays. Day one thousand fifty-eight, done.

howItsDone: In Japanese Zen, monasteries and practice groups keep Rohatsu as a week of intensive sitting that ends on the day observed as the Buddha's awakening.

chat.meaning: In the Padhana Sutta, the seeker names Mara's army troop by troop and doesn't get up. Rohatsu plays that scene again.

Rohatsu.meaning: the Zen week of sitting before the day of awakening

Padhana Sutta.meaning: the discourse on striving, a poem about Mara's army

Sutta Nipata.meaning: an early collection of Buddhist poems and discourses

Mara.meaning: the tempter, who leads the army of desire and doubt

sources.ref: Japanese Zen practice of Rohatsu sesshin

notes: Padhana Sutta paraphrased throughout (Fausbøll's 1881 SBE X translation exists but was not quoted from memory). Confirm the list of Mara's army: desires, discontent, hunger and thirst, craving, sloth and torpor, fear, doubt, hypocrisy and obstinacy, gain/fame/honor/ill-gotten renown, self-exaltation and contempt of others. The ordinal numbers are left out on purpose.
Confirm the ending: Mara's lute (vina) falls from under his arm and he vanishes.

The index places Rohatsu 'before December 8'; the script says only 'the week that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening' and avoids the date and any account of the name's meaning. Keeper may wish to add the date.
Day 691 (Bodhi Day) covered the last night and the morning star; this day stays in the middle of the week on purpose.

Editor pass: the line 'the poem's answer isn't to fight' contradicted the poem's own battle imagery; reworded so the seeker breaks the army with wisdom (the unbaked-pot simile, paraphrased; confirm against Fausbøll) and the myth reveal now matches.
